title: The Worry Box
strapline: A little box where a worry can be drawn, whispered or posted away — so no child has to carry it alone.
intent: Children learn that worries are normal, shareable and lighter once they're let out — not something to hide.
Children who can't yet say a worry aloud get another way to express it — drawing it, whispering it, posting it in.
Children experience an adult reliably noticing and gently following up their worry, building trust.
Children develop the language of anxiety and the idea that there are people whose job is to help.
Children take an active step in managing a feeling — naming it and handing part of it over.
implementation: Make or decorate a special box together, with a posting slot and paper and pencils kept beside it.
Explain gently that a worry can be drawn or told to a grown-up and posted in, and that someone will always check it.
Check the box faithfully and follow up every worry with warmth and privacy — a broken promise here breaks trust fast.
Model it yourself — 'I had a little worry, so I told someone' — so children see that grown-ups have worries too and share them.
Pair it with a reassuring script: 'thank you for telling me, that was brave; let's think together about what might help.'
Keep it confidential and be alert — a worry that hints at harm follows your safeguarding procedures immediately.
key_questions: Is there a worry you'd like to draw or tell me about?
What does your worry feel like — big or small?
Who could help us with this worry?
Do you feel a little lighter now you've shared it?
What might make the worry feel smaller?

impact.text: Children know their own feelings have names and can tell a trusted adult they're worried.
Children talk about feelings, what caused them, and what helps them feel better.
Children ask for help with words, and ask what unfamiliar or worrying things mean.
Children begin to regulate big feelings, sharing a worry as a strategy that helps.
Children make marks and drawings with communicated meaning to express a worry.

enhancements: A 'worry monster' soft toy that 'eats' worries posted into its mouth, for children who like a playful frame.
A companion book about worries shared at group time to normalise talking about them.
A quiet check-in slot with each child's key person so worries can also be spoken, not only posted.
A 'good things' box alongside, where children post happy news too, keeping balance.
A shared home-setting worry routine so a child can post worries at home as well.

playing_exploring: Children explore expressing feelings through drawing and posting, a safe hands-on outlet.
The playful box makes sharing a worry approachable rather than daunting.
active_learning: Feeling lighter after sharing rewards children for reaching out, building the habit.
Children take an active role in managing their feelings rather than bottling them.
creating_thinking: Children connect naming and sharing a worry with feeling better.
They begin to think about who can help and what might make a worry smaller.
